Why Every AI Implementation Strategy Needs a Mast
I saw the new Odyssey movie the other day, and halfway through, it hit me: one of the oldest stories we have is playing out in companies right now, with AI.
Hear me out. In Homer’s classic epic, our hero Odysseus wants to hear the Sirens sing. Their song promises godlike knowledge — and the promise is genuine, which is what makes it so lethal. Every sailor who steered toward that song wrecked on the rocks. Odysseus wants the reward without the ruin, so he engages with the song on his own terms: he has his crew lash him to the mast and plug their own ears with wax, and he gives one order before the singing starts: “No matter how much I beg, do not change course.” In other words, he builds himself a structure.
He hears the song. But the ship stays off the rocks. The discipline was in the timing: he bound himself before the first note.
AI has a similar pull, and it works on smart people for the same reason: the promise is genuine. The gains (speed, efficiency, capability) are within reach, and a true promise pulls harder than an empty one. AI lets you skip the slow, unglamorous part of working out what your problem is, and jump straight to building something impressive. A working demo by Friday. A board slide that says the transformation is underway. The song is lovely, and steering toward it feels like progress.
Then the quarter turns, and a striking share of these projects fizzle out after the pilot. Gartner has put that number at over 50%, and its own reading of why is worth sitting with: the projects stall on unclear value and missing foundations, rather than on the technology falling short. The model usually works; the problem it was aimed at had never been properly defined.
Refusing the song outright means missing what it offers; steering straight for it means the rocks. The third path is the mast, the structure worth binding yourself to before you reach for the tool.
The wreck
Here is how the wreck usually plays out. A capable team stands up a capable system on top of a process that had been named but never mapped, and within a few months the system is shelfware. When someone later says “the AI project failed,” what actually happened was simpler: there was no clear process to encode in the first place.
I saw a version of this unfold recently. A company under pressure to show movement on AI asked their operations director to pilot an AI assistant that would handle inbound customer requests. The trouble was that “handling inbound requests” had never been a defined process. It was a dozen people making reasonable judgment calls in a dozen slightly different ways, held together by tribal knowledge. The pilot automated a snapshot of that improvisation. It demoed beautifully for six weeks. Then the exceptions piled up, the team drifted back to email, and nothing came of it.
Automation is a multiplier, and multipliers do not care what they multiply. Put a clean, deliberate process in front of one and you scale something good. Put a mess in front of one and you scale the mess, faster and more permanently than before.
The mast
The first move to avoid the wreck is diagnosis: mapping how work moves today and where it snags. That work may feel slow and unglamorous. It’s also critical.
The mast, in practice, is a short filter: three gates, taken in order, before you reach for any tool. A problem has to clear all of them to even count as an AI problem at all.
Gate 1 — Process. Is there a defined process here, and if so, what is it? If the honest answer is that the process lives in a few people’s heads and shifts with the weather, you have found your project — and it’s not the AI. Defining the process is the work. Automating a half-formed one only locks the chaos in place.
Gate 2 — Bottleneck. Is there a bottleneck genuinely worth solving — sizable volume, meaningful cost, or judgment-heavy work that eats your best people’s time? If nothing here is truly constrained, a tool will make a fine process marginally faster, for a return just as marginal. That’s polishing, not fixing. The effort belongs where something is stuck.
Gate 3 — Fit. Is AI even the right instrument? Or would a rule, a script, or plain deterministic automation do the job more cheaply and more reliably? A surprising amount of what gets labeled an “AI problem” is a settled question with a checkable answer. That’s a lookup, not a judgment call. You don’t hire a sommelier to tell you the milk’s expired — the date is printed on the carton. Reserve AI, and language models in particular, for the fuzzy, language-shaped, judgment-heavy problems that truly need it, and only where you have a way to verify what it produces.
Clear all three gates and you have something worth building. Even then, one thing decides whether it lasts: whether the people whose work it touches pick it up and use it. A tool that clears every gate and never lands in the daily work is just a very expensive demo.
The reframe
“Where can we use AI” is the wrong question. It sends whole teams hunting for excuses to deploy something they’ve already decided to buy. The question that gets you farther is harder: what are our problems, and which few of them is AI genuinely the right answer to?
Start narrow. Fix the process. Then, and only where it earns its place, apply the tool. That order is your mast. It lets you hear everything AI is promising right now without steering your organization onto the rocks.
